_note: Strand originals: vertical shorts made from public-domain or freely licensed archive pictures (Wikimedia Commons) and a neural voice. Each beat is one sentence or two, over one picture. 'search' finds candidates on Commons; 'pick' is the chosen file (set after looking at the contact sheet); 'focus' is where the slow zoom ends, as fractions of the picture (x, y).

beats.text: For more than six hundred years, this was London Bridge. For over five centuries, it was the only way across the river in London.

credit.artist:
Print made by: Robert Martin

After: John Norden

beats.text: Work began in 1176, under a priest called Peter of Colechurch, and took thirty-three years. It stood on nineteen narrow arches, set on boat-shaped piers called starlings.
beats.search: Old London Bridge arches starlings engraving
beats.pick: Archway of Old London Bridge RMG PW0767.jpg

beats.text: On top grew a street: shops and houses up to seven storeys high, a chapel to Thomas Becket, and Nonsuch House, made in the Netherlands and put together with wooden pegs.
beats.pick: Nonsuch House on London Bridge.jpg

beats.text: The starlings choked the river, so the tide roared through the arches like a weir. Shooting the bridge by boat was a famous way to drown.
beats.search: Old London Bridge tide rapids painting
beats.pick: Image taken from page 613 of 'Old and New London, etc' (11187967333).jpg

beats.text: At the southern gate, the heads of traitors were dipped in tar and set on spikes. William Wallace's was the first, in 1305.
beats.search: London Bridge heads on spikes gate
beats.pick: Image taken from page 614 of 'Old and New London, etc' (11190274454).jpg

beats.text: It was replaced in 1831 by a new bridge just upstream. Its stone alcoves survive today, in Victoria Park and at Guy's Hospital.
beats.pick: London Bridge Stone Alcove - Victoria Park.jpg

beats.text: Highgate Cemetery opened in 1839, one of seven grand cemeteries ringing Victorian London.
beats.pick: Highgate Cemetery (20848993548).jpg

beats.text: Its most visited grave belongs to Karl Marx. He died in London in 1883. The great bronze head came in 1956, paid for by the Communist Party of Great Britain.
beats.pick: Karl Marx grave at the Highgate Cemetery.jpg

beats.text: A few steps away lies George Eliot, author of Middlemarch, buried under her married name, Mary Ann Cross.
beats.pick: George Eliot grave -Highgate Cemetery, London, England-25May2009.jpg

beats.text: Across Swain's Lane, in the West Cemetery, Michael Faraday, pioneer of electricity, lies in a modest grave, true to his quiet faith.
beats.pick: Faraday Michael grave.jpg

beats.text: And Douglas Adams, author of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, where visitors still leave pens beside his headstone.
beats.pick: Grave of Douglas Adams, Highgate Cemetery 2016-06-09.jpg

beats.text: Walk the Egyptian Avenue and the Circle of Lebanon, and you'll see why Victorians came here simply to stroll.
beats.pick: Egyptian Avenue Highgate Cemetery.jpg

beats.text: This broken slab of dark stone is one of the most visited objects in the British Museum: the Rosetta Stone.
beats.pick: 20180506 103138-rosetta-stone.jpg

beats.text: French soldiers found it in 1799, rebuilding a fort near the town of Rosetta, in Egypt's Nile Delta.
beats.pick: The Holman new self-pronouncing Sunday-school teachers Bible (1895) (14793321773).jpg

beats.text: When Britain defeated the French in Egypt, it came to London as a prize of war. It has been on show here since 1802.
beats.pick: Steen van Rosetta, GDE000987.jpg

beats.text: Its secret: it says the same thing three times. In hieroglyphs, in Demotic, and in ancient Greek. It is a royal decree, from 196 BC.
beats.pick: British Museum 2024-10-03m.jpg

beats.text: Scholars could read the Greek, and used it to crack the rest. In 1822, Jean-François Champollion announced that he could read hieroglyphs.
beats.pick: Jean-François Champollion, by Léon Cogniet.jpg

beats.text: Look at its sides, and you can still read the words painted on in London: captured in Egypt by the British Army, in 1801.
beats.search: Rosetta Stone side inscription captured British Army
beats.pick: RosettaStone-LeftAndRightSides-BritishMuseum-August21-08.jpg

beats.text: Christopher Wren's dome has crowned the City since 1710. But this is at least the fourth cathedral to stand on this hill.
beats.pick: St. Paul's Cathedral Dome (exterior).jpg

beats.text: Its medieval predecessor, Old St Paul's, was one of the longest churches in Europe, with a spire taller than today's dome, until lightning set it alight in 1561.
beats.pick: Wenceslas Hollar Old St Paul's Cathedral with spire.jpg

beats.text: In September 1666, the Great Fire swept through the City. The old cathedral, wrapped in wooden scaffolding, burned, and its lead roof melted into the streets.
beats.search: Great Fire of London 1666 painting St Paul's
beats.pick: Wenceslaus Hollar - Burning of old St Paul's Cathedral in the Fire of London - B1977.14.17818 - Yale Center for British Art.jpg

beats.text: Wren spent more than thirty years on its replacement. In 1708, his son laid the last stone, at the very top of the lantern.
beats.pick: Christopher Wren by Godfrey Kneller 1711.jpg

beats.text: The dome is really three: a painted inner dome, a hidden brick cone that carries the lantern, and the lead-covered outer dome you see from the street.
beats.search: St Paul's Cathedral dome section drawing
beats.pick: Dome cross section.jpg

beats.text: Wren lies in the crypt. His epitaph says: reader, if you seek his monument, look around you.
beats.pick: St Paul's Cathedral Nave, London, UK - Diliff.jpg

beats.text: Beside St Paul's stands a stone gateway that spent more than a century somewhere else entirely.
beats.pick: Temple Bar Gate in Paternoster Square.jpg

beats.text: Temple Bar marked the western edge of the City of London, on Fleet Street, where the Strand begins. This arch was built after the Great Fire, and is usually credited to Christopher Wren.
beats.pick: ONL (1887) 1.042 - Temple Bar in Dr Johnson's Time.jpg

beats.text: The heads of executed traitors were set on spikes on top of it. The last were Jacobites, after the rising of 1745.
beats.pick: View of the Temple Bar from Paternoster Square - geograph.org.uk - 4017994.jpg

beats.text: By the 1870s it was blocking the traffic, so it was taken down, stone by stone. The brewer Henry Meux rebuilt it as the gateway to his country estate, Theobalds Park.
beats.pick: Temple Bar, Theobald's Park - geograph.org.uk - 7808719.jpg

beats.text: It stood in a Hertfordshire wood for over a century, overgrown and forgotten, until it came home to the City in 2004.
beats.pick: Temple Bar (geograph 2523995).jpg

beats.text: On Fleet Street, a dragon on a pillar still marks the spot where it once stood.
beats.search: Temple Bar Memorial dragon Fleet Street
beats.pick: Temple Bar. City of London Boundary Dragon. C.B. Birch 1880. - 52253786634.jpg

beats.text: A few steps north of St Paul's is a small garden made from old churchyards. Londoners call it Postman's Park, after the post office workers who ate their lunch here.
beats.pick: Memorial to Heroic Self-Sacrifice 20170904 161303 (49767916073).jpg

beats.text: Under a wooden shelter is a wall of tiles, each remembering an ordinary person who died saving someone else.
beats.search: Memorial to Heroic Self-Sacrifice Postman's Park
beats.pick: Memorial to Heroic Self-Sacrifice 20170904 161314 (49768776012).jpg

beats.text: It was the idea of the painter George Frederic Watts. The memorial opened in 1900, and after his death his wife Mary saw more tiles added.
beats.pick: George Frederic Watts (1817-1904) - Self Portrait in Old Age - COMWG 6 - Watts Gallery.jpg

beats.text: Alice Ayres, a nursemaid, saved three children from a burning house in 1885, pushing them to safety on a mattress, before falling herself.
beats.pick: Postman's Park Memorial to Heroic Self Sacrifice.jpg

beats.text: Each tile gives a name, a date, and a few words, in the language of the time. Read a handful, and they stay with you.
beats.search: Watts Memorial tiles Postman's Park Doulton
beats.pick: George Frederic Watts's Memorial to Heroic Self Sacrifice (29881714055).jpg

beats.text: The film Closer made the park famous in 2004. But the tiles tell the story best. Read a few, then look up at St Paul's.
beats.pick: Central Area of Postman's Park, Facing Southeast.jpg
